Write the Prism-side documentation for evaluating Wisp briefings. Repo: /Users/gabe/Projects/prism. Do not touch any other repo. Do not modify Rust code.

## Read first, in this order

1. Prism's own register: `README.md`, `ARCHITECTURE.md`, `docs/SPECIFICATION.md` (skim), `docs/01-core-evaluation-and-vcr-cassettes.md`, `docs/02-the-four-grader-engines.md`, `docs/04-multi-dimensional-matrix-and-differentials.md`, `docs/05-lumen-integration-and-closed-loop-flywheel.md`. Understand Prism's vocabulary — cassettes, graders, matrix, differentials — so the new doc uses it rather than inventing parallel terms.
2. The requirements: `/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-gabe-Projects-wisp/b57e95d8-2376-4482-beca-d095c103becd/scratchpad/research/03-context-selection.md` (findings 7, 8, 9, 10, 12; the verdict on proposal 16; recommendations 1, 4, 7; the contradictions list), `/Users/gabe/Projects/wisp/docs/03-delivery-plan.md` (Milestone 3 gate, evaluation plan), `/Users/gabe/Projects/wisp/docs/04-decisions-and-open-questions.md` (D-018, D-019, D-020, Q-013), `/Users/gabe/Projects/wisp/docs/02-architecture-and-contracts.md` (context compiler: briefing contract, selection policy, budget policy).

## Write

**`docs/06-wisp-briefing-evaluation.md`** — how Prism evaluates whether a Wisp briefing helps. Content:

- **Two tiers**, as a table: intrinsic (deterministic, per commit, no model run — scores the emitted briefing against ground truth) and extrinsic (paired agent runs — expensive, confirms).
- **Ground truth**: SWE-Explore's method — the code regions that independent successful trajectories actually consulted, distilled per issue; core vs optional regions. How Prism obtains this for Wisp's task suite (plan-task fixtures with known changed lines), and the honest limitation that Wisp's workload (implement one plan task against declared files) may be more structurally determined than SWE-bench issues.
- **Intrinsic metrics**, as a table with formula and why: line-level Recall `|L(P)∩Y|/|Y|` (file-level is solved at ~0.65; agents sit at 0.15–0.19 line recall, so report both and don't let file-level stand in); HitFile/HitRegion; nDCG@B with gain = core lines a region covers, `log2(i+2)` discount, regions in emitted order (this scores Wisp's *ordering* claim); Context Efficiency = fraction of emitted lines inside core ∪ optional (punishes padding to budget); budget sweep at B ∈ {100, 300, 500} lines or token equivalent; α-exposure sweep (vary fraction of ground-truth evidence included, find where resolve jumps) to calibrate the default budget rather than guess.
- **Extrinsic design**, copied from "Code Isn't Memory" (arXiv 2606.22417): hold the model constant; same harness with and without Wisp (SC-ON/SC-OFF); one independent baseline harness; ≥3 seeds; per-cell wall-clock cap; report p-values; headline cost per *solved* task while showing cost per run (their $2.30 vs $2.84 per solve with $/cell p=0.73). State plainly that within-harness is the defensible claim and their cross-harness comparison was not significant (p=0.087, 0.080).
- **Named experiments Wisp has committed to running**, as a table `| Experiment | Arms | Metric | Why it's open |`: section ordering (governing-first vs reverse — position sensitivity doesn't reproduce cleanly on current models and no study tests a headed structured document); 1 vs 3 MCP tools (no ablation exists below ~30 tools; D-019 rests on product precedent); route-count ranking (Q-013: does multi-route support predict usefulness); global cap with floors vs flat ranking (D-018 rests on inference from SWE-Explore, no direct ablation); truncation-marker phrasing (JetBrains showed masking helps; nobody compared marker formats).
- **Reference points** table: Agentless $0.70 / 78,166 tokens per issue (32.00% SWE-bench Lite); LocAgent $0.09–$0.66/example; Nemotron-CORTEXA $3.28/problem (68.2% Verified); SuperCoder $2.30 per solve; RepoGraph 1-hop 29.67% vs 2-hop flattened 26.00% vs baseline 27.33%.
- **The rule**: a smaller briefing is an improvement only if correctness holds (Wisp docs/03). Lumen inspects trajectories for retrieval/tool cycles (Prism doc 05's flywheel) — link it.
- Map each tier onto Prism's existing machinery: which grader engine scores intrinsic metrics, how the matrix expresses arms × seeds × budgets, how cassettes make the extrinsic tier replayable.

Also: add the new doc to `README.md`'s docs list/table and to `docs/SPECIFICATION.md` if it indexes the docs; add a short "Wisp" row wherever `ARCHITECTURE.md` lists consumers or integrations, if such a list exists.

## Style

Match Prism's existing docs. Never hard-wrap lines. Tables for anything with ≥3 rows. One mermaid diagram if it earns its place — the two-tier flow: fixture → Wisp brief → intrinsic scoring (per commit, CI) and → paired harness runs → cassettes → graders → differential. No emoji. Preserve every number and citation; invent nothing. Remove any of: leverage, delve, robust, seamless, crucially, "worth noting", "note that", "in order to", comprehensive, empower, streamline, holistic, "load-bearing", genuinely, materially.

Finish with `git -C /Users/gabe/Projects/prism status --porcelain` and return ≤200 words: what you wrote, how you mapped tiers onto Prism's graders/matrix/cassettes, anything flagged. Do not commit.

input.prompt:
Write the Lumen-side documentation for the telemetry Wisp and Monokl will emit and what Lumen does with it. Repo: /Users/gabe/Projects/lumen. Do not touch any other repo. Do not modify Rust code.

## Read first, in this order

1. Lumen's own register: `README.md`, `ARCHITECTURE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `docs/01-canonical-model-and-economics.md`, `docs/02-streaming-ingestion-and-adapters.md`, `docs/03-22-accumulators-and-analytics.md`, `docs/04-trajectory-dag-and-loop-detection.md`, `docs/06-sqlite-store-and-daemon-architecture.md`. Understand Lumen's vocabulary — canonical model, adapters, accumulators, trajectory DAG, loop detection — and its event/session shapes, so the new doc plugs into them rather than inventing parallels. Look at `crates/lumen-model/src/` for the actual event types.
2. The requirements: `/Users/gabe/Projects/wisp/docs/02-architecture-and-contracts.md` (evidence model, freshness model, cache validity, context compiler budget policy, Lumen row in ecosystem integration), `/Users/gabe/Projects/wisp/docs/04-decisions-and-open-questions.md` (D-008, D-011, D-012, D-013, D-014, D-018), `/Users/gabe/Projects/monokl/docs/spec/08-library-session-api.md` §2 (`Workspace`/`Snapshot`, `ChangeSummary`, `CacheStats`), §7 (`BudgetReport`, `OpBudget`, `OpOutcome`, `SkipReason`), §8.2 (`Provenance`), §13 (benchmarks), and these research findings: `/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-gabe-Projects-wisp/b57e95d8-2376-4482-beca-d095c103becd/scratchpad/research/03-context-selection.md` findings 14–16 (JetBrains masking numbers; Manus: KV-cache hit rate is "the single most important metric", 10× cost difference, 100:1 input:output; stable-prefix ordering), `/private/tmp/.../research/04-incremental-indexing.md` finding 11 (git subprocess cost measurements) and recommendation 1 (moon's `AffectedState` — record *why*), `/private/tmp/.../research/06-artifact-freshness.md` finding 5 (audited silence — snoozes are logged) and recommendation 5 (instrument the rev-walk budget, Callisto's `REVWALK_VISIT_COUNT`).

## Write

**`docs/11-wisp-and-monokl-telemetry.md`** (continue Lumen's numbering) — what Wisp and Monokl emit, and what Lumen measures from it. Content:

- **Boundary**, first: Lumen is an evaluation/telemetry companion, never project truth. Transcripts and Lumen-derived observations never enter Wisp's canonical knowledge without explicit consent and a separate provenance class (Wisp docs/02). Wisp emits sanitized `tracing` events — no raw file contents, no artifact bodies, no secrets — that Lumen correlates. Say what "sanitized" excludes.
- **Event catalogue**, as a table `| Event | Fields | Emitted by | Why Lumen wants it |`, covering at least: brief cache hit/miss with *which input digest moved* on miss (Wisp D-011: validity is the conjunction of input digests, so a miss names the culprit); `Snapshot::is_current` / `provenance_is_current` outcomes and the reason (fingerprint, config hash, or input digest mismatch); `EvidenceFreshness` and `ArtifactFreshness` class per link in a briefing; truncation record per briefing — per category, omitted-for-budget vs omitted-below-floor, expansion query; Monokl `BudgetReport` per batch — tokens/bytes used, per-op `items_returned`/`items_total`, `detail_degraded`, `OpOutcome` skipped reasons (`BudgetExhausted`, `Unsupported`, `Deadline`, `NotIndexed`); Monokl `ChangeSummary` (files re-analyzed vs cache hits) and `CacheStats` on flush; git subprocess count and wall time per `wisp` invocation (measured floor ~8ms/spawn; target is one per invocation); rev-walk commits visited per freshness computation; `commit_declined` receipts and suppressed freshness warnings (audited silence); `AffectedBy` reasons on `wisp impact` edges; scope (`Complete`/`Partial`) and precision per code-evidence item.
- **Headline metrics Lumen computes**, as a table: KV-cache hit rate for harness sessions that consume successive briefings (Manus: single most important production metric; ~10× cost between cached and uncached input tokens; which briefing sections are byte-stable across invocations and therefore cache-eligible — this is why Wisp puts session-stable sections first); tokens per briefing vs task outcome (joined with Prism); retrieval/tool-loop detection over Wisp's `next_actions` follow-up queries — an agent re-issuing the same expansion query is a loop (this is Lumen's trajectory DAG applied to Wisp); stale-context incidents (agent acted on evidence whose freshness class was `CleanBehind`/`DirtyAffected`/`Diverged`); cost per briefing broken into git / Monokl / compile; cache affinity over a session (fraction of briefings served warm).
- **Event shapes reference `orin-contracts`** (`Provenance`, `Digest`, `BudgetReport`, `CapabilityPrecision`) — Lumen's adapter for Wisp/Monokl depends on that permissive crate, not on `wisp-model` or `monokl-core`. State the dependency direction.
- **How this plugs into Lumen**: which adapter ingests it (streaming `tracing` subscriber vs file), which accumulators it feeds, how it lands in the SQLite store, and how the trajectory DAG represents a briefing → follow-up-query chain. Use Lumen's actual type and module names from the docs/source you read.
- **What Lumen does not do here**: no judgment about whether a briefing was *correct* — that's Prism (link Prism's `docs/05-lumen-integration-and-closed-loop-flywheel.md` and Wisp's D-020).

Also: add the new doc to `README.md`'s docs list and to `ARCHITECTURE.md` wherever it lists integrations or upstream producers; add a Wisp/Monokl row to any adapter table in `docs/02-streaming-ingestion-and-adapters.md` if one exists (one row, pointing to the new doc — don't rewrite that file).

## Style

Match Lumen's existing docs. Never hard-wrap lines. Tables for anything with ≥3 rows. One mermaid diagram if it earns its place — Wisp/Monokl `tracing` events → Lumen adapter → accumulators/store → trajectory DAG → metrics, with the Prism join. No emoji. Preserve every number and name; invent nothing — where Lumen's docs don't name a type, say "adapter" generically rather than guessing. Remove any of: leverage, delve, robust, seamless, crucially, "worth noting", "note that", "in order to", comprehensive, empower, streamline, holistic, "load-bearing", genuinely, materially.

Finish with `git -C /Users/gabe/Projects/lumen status --porcelain` and return ≤200 words: what you wrote, how you mapped events onto Lumen's model/adapters/accumulators, anything flagged. Do not commit.

content.text:
All clean. The only slop/emoji hits are in pre-existing text the writers didn't touch (Michi's older decision entries, Prism's README grader diagram); one `✗` in Lumen doc 11's ASCII dependency-direction sketch, which matches Lumen's own house style. Names are consistent across all five repos — `wisp_brief`/`wisp_artifacts`/`wisp_check`, `monokl-core`/`monokl-agent`, `orin-contracts`, `BudgetReport`, `provenance_is_current`, `EvidenceFreshness`.

## What each repo got

| Repo | New doc | Mapped onto | Real gaps it surfaced |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Michi** | `docs/spec/07-wisp-and-monokl-envelope.md` + decision entry + index | `response.rs` line by line; `Section`/`SectionBody`, `budget()`/`provenance()` slots, widened `PartialSuccess`, `outputSchema` | `orin-contracts` must be an optional `contracts` feature (zero-dep default); widening `PartialSuccess` is semver-major; AC-004 pins `render_json()` to four keys and must be rewritten; Wisp+Monokl aren't two *independent* consumers for the publish gate |
| **Prism** | `docs/06-wisp-briefing-evaluation.md` + README docs table | Intrinsic metrics as deterministic graders in the existing offline `eval-pr.yml` gate; extrinsic on `RedGreenGrader`/`TrajectoryGrader`; arms × seeds × budgets as `[[matrix.configs]]`; cassettes replay graders per-PR at $0 | `Grader::evaluate` takes a `CanonicalTranscript`, not a `Briefing`; `TaskSpec` has no ground-truth-regions slot; `MetricDifferential` lacks seed / p-value / cost-per-solve |
| **Lumen** | `docs/11-wisp-and-monokl-telemetry.md` + README docs table + ARCHITECTURE §5 + one ingestion row | 17-row event catalogue on `RawMessageAccumulator::update_raw`; briefing chains on `TrajectoryGraph::push_tool` so Tarjan SCC flags re-issued expansion queries with no new algorithm | `ground_tool_intent` returns ungrounded for `McpCall`, so a `wisp_brief` call can never form a cycle until the adapter maps expansion queries to `CodeSearch`; no correlation field for out-of-band events; `SessionAdapter::load` returns transcripts, and Wisp events aren't one |

Each writer added a control or constraint the research didn't have (Prism's declared-files-only arm; Michi's feature-gating; Lumen's "expansion queries are the one deliberate inclusion in sanitized events, or loop detection is impossible"). Those are the right kind of pushback.

## Decisions for you

1. **`orin-contracts` needs a repo.** Five repos now depend on it; none hosts it. Standalone `~/Projects/orin-contracts` is my recommendation.
2. **Suite license** (Q-003) — AGPL vs FSL. Michi's feature-gating of `orin-contracts` only works if that crate is permissive, which D-021 already assumes.
3. **"Wisp" name collision** with the agent-plugins ecosystem — still unresolved.
4. **Commit.** Six repos have uncommitted doc work from this session (Wisp, Monokl, Michi, Prism, Lumen; agent-plugins untouched). Monokl and Prism also carry someone else's dirty files — I'd commit only the paths we touched, one commit per repo. Say the word and I'll do it, or you can review first.
What is orin-contracts? Is it the wisp schemas?

Partly. It grew during this session from "where the schemas live" into a shared-vocabulary crate. Worth being precise, because the name is now load-bearing in five repos.

## Where it came from

Your original `docs/04` Q-001 asked where the pinned artifact schemas (`spec@1`, `plan@1`, …) should live, and listed "a small standalone `orin-contracts` package" as option 1. That was the whole idea: a versioned, immutable home for the JSON schemas so Wisp never validates against a mutable `agent-plugins` checkout.

## What it became

The research added a second job. Wisp, Monokl, Michi, and Lumen all need to *agree on the meaning* of a handful of value types that none of them should own:

| Type | Why it can't live in any one repo |
| --- | --- |
| `Digest` (`sha256:`/`blake3:` OCI grammar) | Wisp hashes artifacts, Monokl hashes files, Lumen logs both |
| `CapabilityPrecision` | Monokl produces it, Wisp carries it through, Lumen counts it |
| `Provenance` | Monokl attaches it, Wisp stores and revalidates it, Lumen correlates on it |
| `BudgetReport` / truncation shape | Monokl emits it, Michi renders it, Lumen measures it |
| `SymbolId` grammar + parser | Monokl mints it, Wisp's `code_evidence_refs` must round-trip it — and `wisp-model` is forbidden from depending on Monokl |
| `Diagnostic` (transport shape only) | Every tool emits one |
| The pinned artifact JSON schemas | The original Q-001 answer |

The rule D-010 states: *if Wisp and Monokl must agree on its meaning, contracts; if Monokl computes it, `monokl-core`.* Value types only, serde-derived because they are the wire format, no behavior beyond `Display`/`FromStr`.

## Why it has to be its own thing

- **License.** Monokl and Michi are AGPL. Third-party harness plugins (Python, Node) must be able to read a `spec@1` schema and verify a `sha256:` receipt without copyleft obligations. So the crate is `MIT OR Apache-2.0` — which means it cannot live inside Monokl or Michi.
- **Dependency direction.** `wisp-model` → `orin-contracts` is allowed; `wisp-model` → `monokl-core` is not. Michi wants it as an optional feature so its zero-dep default survives. Lumen's adapter depends on it rather than on `wisp-model`. It's the one leaf everything points at.
- **Versioning.** Schemas are immutable by version; a re-pin to a newer `agent-plugins` revision is a versioned release of this crate. That needs its own release cadence, not Wisp's.

## So: is it "the Wisp schemas"?

The schemas are in it, but they're `agent-plugins`' schemas (Wisp vendors them at revision `b5e2db19…` today). The crate is better described as **the orin-axi interchange vocabulary** — schemas plus the six or seven types that cross process boundaries between the tools. Small, boring, permissive, versioned independently.

If that's more scope than you want, the minimal alternative is: schemas-only crate under the original Q-001 meaning, and each pair of repos hand-writes conversions for `Provenance`/`Digest`/etc. That works but you'd be maintaining the same OCI digest parser in three places. I'd keep the wider scope — it's what the research kept converging on from four independent directions.

Where should it live? Standalone repo is my recommendation; the alternative is a `contracts/` crate inside `agent-plugins`, which already owns the schemas but would then be publishing Rust.
We will steal wisp from the agent plugins. We can call that the Wisp Plugins

Good — that resolves the collision cleanly: this repo is **Wisp** (the library), the ten-plugin ecosystem is **Wisp Plugins**. Let me see how far the old name reaches in `agent-plugins` before editing.

1	# ADR-007: Wisp persona naming — plugin ID rename
2	
3	**Status:** Accepted
4	**Date:** 2026-08-27
5	**Supersedes:** none — this is a naming/identity change, not a structural one. All prior ADRs (001-006) remain in force under the new plugin ids.
6	
7	## Context
8	
9	The ecosystem's plugin ids were abstract math and CS nouns — `graph`, `trace`, `canon`, `vector`, `lambda`, `proof`, `axiom`, `delta`, `basis` — chosen when the ecosystem had a handful of plugins and the words mapped loosely to each plugin's domain concept (a requirement graph, a research trace, an architectural canon, a planning vector, a lambda calculus of implementation, formal proof, a verification axiom, a changeset delta, a basis for scaffolding). As the ecosystem grew past nine plugins, this stopped working as a memory aid. The ids no longer reliably cued which plugin did what: `canon` versus `axiom` versus `basis` gave no intuitive signal about spec-writing versus gating versus scaffolding, and `proof` versus `trace` versus `vector` required already knowing the mapping rather than being able to infer it. New contributors and even experienced users were routing skill invocations by looking up a table rather than by recall. A tenth plugin (component specification) was also being added, compounding the problem — an eleventh abstract noun was not going to help.
10	
11	## Alternatives Considered
12	
13	- **Keep the abstract-noun scheme and add a lookup table to every doc.** Rejected: this treats the symptom (poor discoverability) without fixing the cause (the names carry no intrinsic signal), and a lookup table itself becomes another thing to keep in sync as plugins are added.
14	- **Rename to literal function names** (e.g. `spec-writer`, `bug-hunter`, `verifier`, `planner`). Considered seriously — this maximizes literal clarity. Rejected because several plugins are hard to compress into one literal word without collision (`canon`/spec-writing and `muse`/component-spec-writing would both want "spec-writer"; `axiom` and the exit-gate concept it wraps are hard to name without stealing a word every plugin's own exit-gate agent already uses internally) and because a persona gives room for the skill name to carry the literal action instead, avoiding the collision entirely.
15	- **Persona-based naming**, where the plugin id is a character or craft-role archetype and the *skill* name (not the plugin id) carries the literal action. Accepted — see Decision.
16	
17	## Decision
18	
19	Every plugin id is renamed to a persona — a character or craft-role archetype evocative of that plugin's function — under a single umbrella brand for the whole family: **Wisp**. The literal action moves to the skill name, following the convention `persona:action` (e.g. `ranger:audit`, `sentinel:gate`). For the five single-skill plugins, where the skill name previously duplicated the plugin id, the skill is renamed to the literal action it performs. For the four multi-skill plugins, which already had distinct literal skill names (`draft-spec`, `changeset`, `capture-need`, `scaffold-plugin`, etc.), only the plugin-id prefix changes in any documented invocation — the skill names themselves are unchanged.
20	
21	A tenth plugin, `muse`, is added in the same change: a component-specification plugin (Design category, alongside `scribe`) that turns UI/design intent into testable component specs — props, variants, per-state behavior, accessibility criteria — gated the same way `scribe` gates a spec. It reuses the existing `spec@1`/`verdict@1` schemas unchanged; no new schema was needed.
22	
23	### Full mapping
24	
25	| Old id | New id (persona) | Category | Skill(s) |
26	| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
27	| `graph` | `weaver` | Requirements | `capture-need`, `clarify-requirement`, `prioritize-backlog`, `connect-requirement`, `audit-backlog` (unchanged) |
28	| `trace` | `vanguard` | Research | `research` (was `trace`) |
29	| `canon` | `scribe` | Design | `draft-spec`, `verify-spec`, `spec-drift`, `audit-spec`, `gate-spec`, `correct-spec`, `architect` (unchanged) |
30	| — | `muse` *(new)* | Design | `component` |

# ADR-010: Ecosystem brand becomes "Wisp Plugins"

**Status:** Accepted
**Date:** 2026-09-03
**Supersedes:** the umbrella-brand clause of ADR-007. Plugin ids, skill names, categories, and the `persona:action` convention from ADR-007 are unchanged.

## Context

ADR-007 named the ten-plugin family **Wisp**. Separately, `orin-axi/wisp` is the local-first project-intelligence library these plugins consume — it validates and persists the `spec@1`/`plan@1` artifacts the plugins hand off, and compiles the briefings `smith`, `sentinel`, and `scribe` will read. Two different things carried one name across two repositories, and every cross-reference between them had to disambiguate by hand.

## Decision

- The library keeps **Wisp**.
- The plugin ecosystem is **Wisp Plugins**. This is a brand change only: no `plugin.json` `id`, `name`, or version changes; no skill renames; no schema changes.
- In this repository, "Wisp" alone refers to the library. The ecosystem is written "Wisp Plugins" in prose and headings.
- The repository directory and remote name (`agent-plugins`) are unchanged by this ADR.

## Consequences

- `README.md` and any current-facing doc that says "together they're Wisp" says "Wisp Plugins".
- Historical changelog entries and ADR-007's own text stay as written; they record what the brand was when the rename shipped.
- The Wisp library's docs refer to this ecosystem as "Wisp Plugins (`agent-plugins`)" and pin its schemas through `orin-contracts` (Wisp D-010).

## 11. `orin-contracts`

A small, permissively licensed crate holding vocabulary both monokl and Wisp must agree on the *meaning* of, and that third-party harness plugins (which cannot link AGPL code) need to parse:

- `CapabilityPrecision`
- `Digest`, `DigestAlgorithm`
- `Diagnostic`, `DiagnosticKind` — as the *transport* shape only. Monokl keeps `MonoklError`; Wisp keeps its own domain errors; both convert. A shared diagnostic that tries to be the domain type becomes the lowest-common-denominator collapse [06 §6](./06-daemon-architecture.md) already argues against.
- `Provenance`, `AnalyzerId`, `OperationId`, `InputRef`, `WorkspaceFingerprint`, `Scope`
- `BudgetReport`, `OpBudget`
- `SymbolId` with its grammar, parser, and `Display`
- The pinned artifact JSON schemas (`spec@1`, `plan@1`, …) with their source revision and checksums

The test for inclusion: "must monokl and Wisp agree on what this *means*?" → contracts. "Does monokl *compute* it?" → `monokl-core`. Result types (`SymbolsResult`, `RankedBlock`, `FileAnalysis`) stay in core, unshared and not `Serialize`; their wire counterparts are built in `monokl-agent`.

**Open licensing question**, recorded and not decided here: `SymbolId`'s grammar and parser are the piece of monokl most plausibly considered valuable IP, and this puts them in a permissive crate. The technical argument (Wisp's `wisp-model` may not depend on monokl implementation types, and storing symbols as untyped strings loses the parse) and the licensing instinct point in opposite directions.

## 12. SCIP interop: what we lose

`monokl index --format scip` is a natural later addition. Three things are lossy on export and should not be rediscovered:

| Lost on export | Detail |
| :--- | :--- |
| Per-edge precision (§8.3) | No SCIP encoding. Dropped. |
| `SymbolId::Local` | Degrades to SCIP's `local N`, which is unstable by construction. Emit it only at the boundary. |
| Rust impl encoding | Uses rust-analyzer's `impl#[Self][Trait]` convention, which the SCIP grammar does not sanction. Compatible with rust-analyzer's output; not guaranteed compatible with a future scip-rust. |

## 13. Benchmarks

`benches/pipeline.rs`'s four criterion groups are stubs. Every latency target in this spec — the 15s cold build, the 100–500ms refold at 10k files, the 300ms–1.5s at 50k — is asserted, not measured, and [05 §11](./05-research-and-decisions.md) already calls the cold-build target "unvalidated and plausibly optimistic." The ~50k-file threshold below which a persistent index supposedly doesn't earn its cost has no external corroboration; the nearest data point cuts the other way (CodeGraph persists to SQLite at 4,400 files). This benchmark is the number the whole no-persistent-index architecture rests on, and it is also the number Wisp needs before Milestone 3.

# Round 2: mechanics, seams, and the missing specs

Round 1 (2026-09-03) settled architecture: Wisp D-001..D-021 (`/Users/gabe/Projects/wisp/docs/04-decisions-and-open-questions.md`), Monokl spec 08 (`/Users/gabe/Projects/monokl/docs/spec/08-library-session-api.md`), Michi spec 07, Prism doc 06, Lumen doc 11. Round 2 fills the gaps between decisions and buildable specs.

## Naming (fixed)

- **Wisp** — the library (`~/Projects/wisp`). Crates `wisp-model`, `wisp-schema`, `wisp-artifacts`, `wisp-git`, `wisp-monokl`, `wisp-store`, `wisp-context`, `wisp-output`, `wisp-service`, `wisp-cli`, `wisp-mcp`, `wisp-fixtures`.
- **Wisp Plugins** — the ten-plugin agent ecosystem (`~/Projects/agent-plugins`). Authors the artifact JSON schemas.
- **`wisp-contracts`** — permissive crate of cross-repo *vocabulary* types: `Digest`, `CapabilityPrecision`, `Diagnostic` (transport shape), `Provenance` (+ `AnalyzerId`, `OperationId`, `InputRef`, `WorkspaceFingerprint`, `Scope`), `BudgetReport`/`OpBudget`, `SymbolId` grammar+parser. **No schemas.** Consumed by Wisp, Monokl, Michi (optional feature), Lumen. No repo exists yet.
- **Monokl** — `monokl-core` (plumbing) / `monokl-agent` (porcelain). **Michi** — envelope/rendering. **Lumen** — telemetry. **Prism** — evaluation. **Callisto** — release engine, and `callisto-vcs`/`callisto-model` are MIT/Apache-2.0 and reusable.

## Known contradictions and gaps to resolve (assigned per track)

1. **Budget seam.** Monokl 08 §7 puts `budget: Budget` and `BudgetPolicy` on `Snapshot::query(&QueryRequest)` in `monokl-core`, but §9 puts `apply_budget`, tiktoken, and `Detail` degrade in `monokl-agent`. Resolve: what does core measure (bytes? item counts?), what does agent measure (tokens), and how does Wisp — a consumer of core, not agent — get a token-bounded batch without depending on agent's tiktoken? Options: core budgets in bytes and returns counts; agent converts tokens→bytes; or `Budget` is a trait object with a `measure(&[u8]) -> usize` the caller supplies. Pick one with reasons.
2. **Declared paths per artifact type.** `EvidenceFreshness` (Wisp docs/02 §4.2) needs "declared paths" per artifact-link. `plan@1` tasks carry `files.create/modify/test`; `spec@1` carries none; `arch-model@1` carries module boundaries; `requirement@1` carries nothing. Define the derivation rule per type, and what freshness means for an artifact with no declared paths (inherit from linked plan? `Indeterminate { NoDeclaredPaths }`?).
3. **`wisp brief` end-to-end.** No sequence exists. Wisp has no latency targets at all.
4. **Error taxonomy across boundaries.** Monokl `.claude/semantic-model/error-taxonomy.md` exists (someone's in-progress work — read, don't edit). Wisp has none. `Diagnostic` transport shape in `wisp-contracts` is named, not defined.
5. **Typed `Briefing`.** Sections are a table in docs/02 §9.1, not types. `Evidence<T>` has no catalogue of `T`. `AffectedBy` is a name.
6. **Threading.** `Snapshot: Send + Sync + 'static`; rayon inside `Workspace::open`; tokio in `wisp-service`/`wisp-mcp`. Where is `spawn_blocking`? Can two tokio tasks share one `Snapshot`? Does `apply_change(&mut self)` need a `Mutex<Workspace>` in the service, and what does that do to concurrent readers?
7. **Polyrepo mechanics.** Six repos, path dependencies during development (Michi D-006 precedent), `wisp-contracts` versioned independently, Callisto as release engine. How do CI and local builds resolve `monokl-core` before it's published? `[patch.crates-io]`? A `Cargo.toml` workspace-of-workspaces? git submodules? What does Callisto need to release a polyrepo set in dependency order?
8. **Michi `telemetry` module** (`NoopProvider`, "zero-cost default, always compiled" — see Michi `AGENTS.md` module guide) is an existing seam. Lumen doc 11 specified an adapter without using it. Reconcile.
9. **Monokl parallel work.** `~/Projects/monokl/.claude/specs/SPEC-004.json`, `SPEC-005.json`, `SPEC-009..011.json`, `.claude/plans/PLAN-001..010.json`, `.claude/plans/ACTIVE.md`, `.claude/semantic-model/error-taxonomy.md` are someone else's uncommitted, in-flight work. Spec 08 was written without reading them. Conflicts must be found before anyone builds either.
10. **Q-005 workspace configuration** — filename, discovery, defaults, fingerprint contribution. Open.
11. **Cross-repo integration fixtures** — a fixture repo Wisp+Monokl both run against. Location and shape undefined.

## Output contract

Write to the path in your brief. Markdown, **never wrap lines**, succinct, engineering register, tables for ≥3 rows, real Rust signatures where you propose types, no emoji, no filler words (leverage, delve, robust, seamless, crucially, comprehensive, genuinely, materially, "note that", "in order to"). Structure: `## Sources read` (path/URL + `confirmed`/`likely`), `## Findings`, `## Proposal` (the concrete spec text or type definitions, ready to paste into the target doc), `## Conflicts with existing docs` (quote the line, say what changes), `## Open`. Return ≤250 words to the caller. Do not modify any repo — outputs are integrated after review.

358	Three reasons the budget belongs to the caller, in decreasing weight.
359	
360	1. **Wisp budgets across categories Monokl cannot see.** One global cap spans governing artifacts, criteria, invariants, code evidence, Git evidence, risks, and truncation (§9.4). A Monokl-side token budget is at best a sub-budget of that, so Wisp would have to guess the code split before knowing what the artifact sections cost, then measure the returned bytes again to place them against reserved floors. That is two passes plus a round trip to fix a bad guess; caller-side budgeting is one pass.
361	2. **A caller-supplied measure closure cannot be digested.** `OperationId { op, normalized_params: Digest }` has no way to represent a `Box<dyn Fn(&str) -> usize>`, so two requests with identical ops and different measures would share an `OperationId` and `provenance_is_current` would call a stale cached result current.
362	3. **No tokens-per-byte constant is both safe and useful.** Rust source measures 3.78 bytes per token; the adversarial worst case is 1.0. A constant of 3.78 overruns by up to 3.8× on minified or control-character-dense content, and a constant of 1.0 is the byte bound with extra ceremony.
363	
364	Core keeps only `Limits { max_items_per_op, max_bytes_per_op }`, framed as a memory guard, with `items_total` reporting what the ceiling cut.
365	
366	**Byte length is an exact upper bound on token count, not a heuristic.** All 256 single-byte tokens are present in both `cl100k_base` and `o200k_base`; BPE never splits below a byte and every merge strictly reduces the count, so a pretoken of *k* bytes encodes to between 1 and *k* tokens. The measured worst case is exactly 1.000 tokens per byte and never above. So `remaining_budget >= s.len()` admits an item under any measure with the tokenizer never invoked — a prefilter with zero false negatives, which on ordinary source admits the great majority of items for free.

370	    fn id(&self) -> MeasureId;
371	    /// Exact count under this measure. May be expensive.
372	    fn count(&self, s: &str) -> usize;
373	    /// A cheap ceiling: `count(s) <= upper_bound(s)` for every `s`. Never approximate downward.
374	    fn upper_bound(&self, s: &str) -> usize { s.len() }
375	}
376	```

378	`ByteUpperBound` is the default and needs no dependency; it underfills by roughly 3.8× on real code and never overfills. A tokenizer measure must fall back to `upper_bound` above a hard byte cap, because `byte_pair_merge` is quadratic in pretoken length and 200 KB of one unbroken run takes 8.59 s. ### 7.5 Where the budget went

`Budget`, `BudgetPolicy`, `apply_budget`, and tiktoken are **not** in `monokl-core`. Core returns fully ranked, uncapped results plus per-op cost; every budget is allocated one layer up, by `monokl-agent` for the CLI and by Wisp's `wisp-context` for a briefing. Wisp depends on `monokl-core` alone and never links `monokl-agent`, so monokl's CLI, wire types, allocation policy, and tokenizer choice are free to churn without a Wisp release — which is what §9.1 promises porcelain.

That needs a round trip — the exact multi-call pattern §7.1 cites Anthropic's 150,000 → 2,000-token result to eliminate. One budgeting pass, in the only component that can see every category, is strictly better.
2. **It is the only arrangement that resolves the contradiction rather than relocating it.** §9.1's core box already reads *fully ranked, deduped, uncapped results … no tiktoken … no caps*, while §7.3 previously put a `Budget` on a core request type and §7.2's own diagram labelled `apply_budget` a `monokl-agent` step inside a `monokl-core` method. ---
name: project-wisp-naming
description: Wisp naming, wisp-contracts location, licensing model, and cross-repo release order (decided 2026-09-03/04)
metadata:
  type: project
---

**Names.** `~/Projects/wisp` is **Wisp** (the library). The ten-plugin ecosystem in `~/Projects/agent-plugins` is **Wisp Plugins** (ADR-010 there). **`wisp-contracts`** is the cross-repo vocabulary crate (`Digest`, `Provenance`, `CapabilityPrecision`, `SymbolId`, `BudgetReport`/`OpBudget`/`OpCost`, transport `Diagnostic`). It holds **no artifact schemas** — those stay in Wisp Plugins `shared/schemas/` and Wisp vendors them at a pinned revision. Only Wisp and Wisp Plugins consume schemas.

**Location (2026-09-04).** `wisp-contracts` is a crate *inside the Wisp workspace* (`crates/wisp-contracts`), published from there with its own version. No separate repo. Wisp owns its cadence.

**Licensing (2026-09-04).** Template is Lumen + Callisto, not Michi: `wisp-contracts` and `wisp-model` are **MIT**; every other Wisp crate is **FSL-1.1-MIT** (Lumen's flavor). `SymbolId` ships MIT. Michi and Monokl are AGPL-3.0-or-later today; an FSL crate linking AGPL is a redistribution conflict, so relicensing both to FSL-1.1-MIT before first publish is the expected path — Gabe's call in those repos.

content.text:
# Fewer Permission Prompts

Look through my transcripts' MCP and bash tool calls, and based on those, make a prioritized list of patterns that I should add to my permission allowlist to reduce permission prompts. Focus on read-only commands.

The format for permissions is: `Bash(foo*)`, `Bash(foo)`, `Bash(foo bar *)`, `mcp__slack__slack_read_thread`, etc.

Then, add these to the project `.claude/settings.json` under `permissions.allow`.

## Steps

1. **Locate transcripts.** Session transcripts live at `~/.claude/projects/<sanitized-cwd>/*.jsonl`. Each line is a JSON object. Tool calls appear as `assistant` messages with `message.content[]` entries of `type: "tool_use"`. The `name` field identifies the tool (e.g. `"Bash"`, `"mcp__slack__slack_read_thread"`); for Bash, `input.command` is the shell string.

   Scan the recent transcripts across the user's projects dir — not just the current project — so the allowlist reflects their actual usage. Cap the scan at a reasonable number of recent sessions (e.g. 50 most-recently-modified JSONL files) so this stays fast.

2. **Extract tool-call frequencies.**
   - For `Bash` calls: parse `input.command`, take the leading command token (handling `sudo`, `timeout`, pipes, `&&`, env-var prefixes). Record the command + first subcommand pair (e.g. `git status`, `gh pr view`, `ls`, `cat`).
   - For MCP calls: record the full tool name (e.g. `mcp__slack__slack_read_thread`).
   - Count occurrences across the scanned transcripts.

3. **Filter to read-only.** Keep only commands that don't mutate state. Examples of read-only: `ls`, `cat`, `pwd`, `git status`, `git log`, `git diff`, `git show`, `git branch`, `rg`, `grep`, `find`, `head`, `tail`, `wc`, `file`, `which`, `echo`, `date`, `gh pr view`, `gh pr list`, `gh pr diff`, `gh issue view`, `gh issue list`, `gh run list`, `gh run view`, `gh api` (GET), `bun run typecheck`, `bun run lint`, `bun run test` (for tests that don't mutate), `docker ps`, `docker logs`, `kubectl get`, `kubectl describe`, `ps`, `top`, `df`, `du`, `env`, `printenv`, any MCP tool with `read`/`get`/`list`/`search`/`view` in its name.

   Drop anything that writes, deletes, renames, pushes, merges, installs, or runs a build/test that has side effects. When in doubt, leave it out.

   **Never allowlist a pattern that grants arbitrary code execution.** A wildcard rule for any of these (e.g. `Bash(python3:*)`) is equivalent to allowing arbitrary code execution. This list is not exhaustive — apply the same rule to anything in the same category:
   - Interpreters: `python`/`python3`, `node`, `bun`, `deno`, `ruby`, `perl`, `php`, `lua`, etc.
   - Shells: `bash`, `sh`, `zsh`, `fish`, `eval`, `exec`, `ssh`, etc.
   - Package runners: `npx`, `bunx`, `uvx`, `uv run`, etc.
   - Task-runner wildcards: `npm run *`, `yarn run *`, `pnpm run *`, `bun run *`, `make *`, `just *`, `cargo run *`, `go run *`, etc. — an exact `Bash(bun run typecheck)` is fine, `Bash(bun run *)` is not
   - `gh api *`, `docker run`/`exec`, `kubectl exec`, `sudo`, and similar

4. **Drop commands Claude Code already auto-allows.** These don't need an allowlist entry — they never prompt. If you see any of these in the transcripts, skip them; don't suggest them to the user.

   - **Always auto-allowed (any args):** `cal`, `uptime`, `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `wc`, `stat`, `strings`, `hexdump`, `od`, `nl`, `id`, `uname`, `free`, `df`, `du`, `locale`, `groups`, `nproc`, `basename`, `dirname`, `realpath`, `cut`, `paste`, `tr`, `column`, `tac`, `rev`, `fold`, `expand`, `unexpand`, `fmt`, `comm`, `cmp`, `numfmt`, `readlink`, `diff`, `true`, `false`, `sleep`, `which`, `type`, `expr`, `seq`, `tsort`, `pr`, `echo`, `ls`, `cd`.
   - **Auto-allowed with zero args only:** `pwd`, `whoami`, `alias`.
   - **Auto-allowed exact forms:** `claude -h`, `claude --help`, `node -v`, `node --version`, `python --version`, `python3 --version`, `ip addr`.
   - **Auto-allowed with safe flags only (validated):** `xargs`, `file`, `sed` (read-only expressions), `sort`, `man`, `help`, `netstat`, `ps`, `base64`, `grep`, `egrep`, `fgrep`, `sha256sum`, `sha1sum`, `md5sum`, `tree`, `date`, `hostname`, `lsof`, `pgrep`, `tput`, `ss`, `fd`, `fdfind`, `aki`, `rg`, `jq`, `uniq`, `history`, `arch`, `ifconfig`, `pyright`, `find` (blocks `-delete`/`-exec`/`-execdir`/`-ok`/`-okdir`/`-fprint*`/`-fls`/`-files0-from`), `printf` (blocks any `-flag`), `test` (blocks `-v`/`-R`/`-a`/`-o`).
   - **All git read-only subcommands:** `git status`, `git log`, `git diff`, `git show`, `git blame`, `git branch`, `git tag`, `git remote`, `git ls-files`, `git ls-remote`, `git config --get`, `git rev-parse`, `git describe`, `git stash list`, `git reflog`, `git shortlog`, `git cat-file`, `git for-each-ref`, `git worktree list`, etc.
   - **All gh read-only subcommands:** `gh pr view`, `gh pr list`, `gh pr diff`, `gh pr checks`, `gh pr status`, `gh issue view`, `gh issue list`, `gh issue status`, `gh run view`, `gh run list`, `gh workflow list`, `gh workflow view`, `gh repo view`, `gh release view`, `gh release list`, `gh api` (GET), `gh auth status`, etc.
   - **Docker read-only subcommands:** `docker ps`, `docker images`, `docker logs`, `docker inspect`.

   Source of truth: `src/tools/BashTool/readOnlyValidation.ts` (`READONLY_COMMANDS`, `READONLY_NOARGS`, `READONLY_EXACT`, `COMMAND_ALLOWLIST`) and `src/utils/shell/readOnlyCommandValidation.ts` (`GIT_READ_ONLY_COMMANDS`, `GH_READ_ONLY_COMMANDS`, `DOCKER_READ_ONLY_COMMANDS`, `RIPGREP_READ_ONLY_COMMANDS`, `PYRIGHT_READ_ONLY_COMMANDS`). If the user is in this repo and you're unsure whether a command is covered, grep these files rather than guessing.

5. **Pick the pattern form.** Use the narrowest pattern that still covers the observed usage:
   - If the user runs many variants (`git log`, `git log --oneline`, `git log main..HEAD`): use `Bash(git log *)` — note the space before `*`, which is required for prefix matching to work correctly.
   - If a single exact invocation is common: use `Bash(foo)` with no wildcard.
   - For MCP: use the full tool name verbatim (no wildcard needed; they're already specific).
   - Never widen a pattern to the point that it conflicts with the rules above (no arbitrary code execution, no mutation/side effects).

6. **Prioritize.** Rank by count descending. Drop anything that appeared fewer than ~3 times — not worth the allowlist entry. Cap the list at the top ~20 so the user can skim it.

7. **Present the prioritized list to the user** as a markdown table with columns: rank, pattern, count, one-line description. Example:

   | # | Pattern | Count | Notes |
   |---|---------|-------|-------|
   | 1 | `Bash(git status *)` | 142 | repo status checks |
   | 2 | `Bash(gh pr view *)` | 87 | PR inspection |
   | 3 | `mcp__slack__slack_read_thread` | 54 | Slack thread reads |

8. **Merge into `.claude/settings.json`** in the current project (not `~/.claude/settings.json`, not `.claude/settings.local.json`). Create the file if it doesn't exist. Preserve existing keys and existing entries in `permissions.allow`; de-duplicate against what's already there; don't remove anything; don't reorder unrelated fields.

9. **Report back.** Tell the user what you added (count + a few examples), what was already in the allowlist, and what you skipped and why (e.g. "dropped `rm` and `git push` — not read-only; dropped `cat`/`ls`/`git status` — already auto-allowed, no rule needed").

Do not add anything to `permissions.deny` or `permissions.ask`. Do not touch any other settings field.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Lint the repository's markdown against the house style: no filler words, balanced
# code fences, every D-/Q- reference defined in the decision log, no stale names.
# Read-only. Exit 1 on any finding so `just ci-fast` can gate on it.
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(dirname "$0")/.."

files=$(git ls-files --cached --others --exclude-standard -- '*.md' | grep -v -E '^(target|node_modules|docs/research|docs/projects|docs/specs|docs/requirements)/')
status=0

echo "== filler words =="
if rg -n -i '\b(leverage|delve|robust|seamless|crucially|worth noting|in order to|comprehensive|cutting-edge|empower|streamline|holistic|synerg|genuinely|materially)\b' $files | grep -v -i -E 'OCI|verbatim|quot'; then status=1; else echo none; fi

echo "== emoji =="
if rg -n -P '[\x{1F300}-\x{1FAFF}]' $files | grep -v 'local 🧠'; then status=1; else echo none; fi

echo "== unbalanced code fences =="
odd=0
for f in $files; do
  n=$(grep -c '^```' "$f" || true)
  if [ $((n % 2)) -ne 0 ]; then echo "$f"; odd=1; fi
done
[ "$odd" -eq 0 ] && echo none || status=1

echo "== D-/Q- references without a definition =="
log=docs/04-decisions-and-open-questions.md
rg -o -I -N 'D-0[0-9]{2}|Q-0[0-9]{2}' $files | sort -u > /tmp/wisp-docs-lint-refs
rg -o -I -N '^### (D|Q)-0[0-9]{2}' "$log" | rg -o '(D|Q)-0[0-9]{2}' | sort -u > /tmp/wisp-docs-lint-defs
# Questions closed by a decision are referenced but have no heading; list them here.
resolved='Q-001 Q-002 Q-003 Q-004 Q-005 Q-006 Q-010 Q-014 Q-015'
missing=$(comm -23 /tmp/wisp-docs-lint-refs /tmp/wisp-docs-lint-defs | grep -v -x -F -f <(printf '%s\n' $resolved) || true)
if [ -n "$missing" ]; then echo "$missing"; status=1; else echo none; fi

echo "== stale names =="
if rg -n -i 'orin[-_]contracts|state\.sqlite|\.wisp/config\.toml|wisp_impact\b|wisp_status\b|wisp_verify\b|CLI adapter phase' $files | grep -v -i -E 'no CLI|not a CLI|never|was |formerly|earlier draft'; then status=1; else echo none; fi

exit $status

## What this is

Spec Part 8 (`docs/spec/08-library-session-api.md`): the embedded-library API Wisp depends on, and the FSL-1.1-MIT relicense. Documentation and license metadata only; no Rust changes.

## Why

`pipeline::search/symbols/dependents` each build their own analyzer and index per call, `WorkspaceIndex::build` is `pub(crate)`, and every op flushes the disk cache. A consumer embedding monokl in-process pays a full walk ten times for ten ops. Part 8 replaces that with `Workspace` + `Snapshot`, a transactional `apply_change`, and a batch `query` that runs against one revision.

## What to review

| Section | Claim | Evidence to check |
| --- | --- | --- |
| §2–3 | Two types, no cancellation | rust-analyzer needs cancellation only because Salsa's memo table is shared mutable storage; monokl's index is immutable after build |
| §4 | `FileIdx` must stop being positional before scoped open or `apply_change` | `ImportGraph.reverse` keys on it today |
| §5 | Scope is orthogonal to precision; `dependents`/`refs` return `Unsupported` under `Partial` | Every scoped precedent (Kythe, TS project refs, `cargo check -p`) breaks on the reverse closure |
| §7 | Core returns uncapped ranked results + `OpCost`; the caller budgets | A closure has no digest; no safe bytes/token ratio; byte length is an exact token upper bound |
| §8 | `SymbolId` has no path, kind, or line | SCIP grammar and `DESIGN.md`, read in full |
| §9 | `monokl-core` / `monokl-agent` split; no `Serialize` on core types | rust-analyzer's `ide` invariant |
| §13 | Every latency target is unmeasured; the ~50k crossover has no external corroboration | `benches/pipeline.rs` is stubs |
| §14 | SPEC-011 and SPEC-004 are superseded, not reverted | Quoted |
| `LICENSE`, `Cargo.toml`, `deny.toml`, `README.md` | AGPL → FSL-1.1-MIT | Matches Lumen's `LICENSE` text and `deny.toml` shape |

Also: `05-research-and-decisions.md` §15 logs each decision with sources; a gopls citation in `06` is re-sourced; `ARCHITECTURE.md` and `README.md` get Callisto-style diagrams and a license section; `AGENTS.md` gains two non-negotiables.

## Not in this PR

Everything under `.claude/` — in-flight specs and plans by another session. `justfile`, `rust-toolchain.toml`, `.moon/`, `.prototools` are pre-existing untracked scaffold.

AgentResponse holds one TOON slot or one KV slot, whichever setter ran last, so a Wisp briefing or a monokl batch result with ten sections silently loses nine. Spec 07 defines the repeatable Section, a BudgetSummary slot, a ProvenanceBlock slot, index-bearing per-op outcomes on PartialSuccess, and outputSchema publication. # ADR-010: Ecosystem brand becomes "Wisp Plugins"

**Status:** Accepted
**Date:** 2026-09-03
**Supersedes:** the umbrella-brand clause of ADR-007. Plugin ids, skill names, categories, and the `persona:action` convention from ADR-007 are unchanged.

## Context

ADR-007 named the ten-plugin family **Wisp**. Separately, `orin-axi/wisp` is the local-first project-intelligence library these plugins consume — it validates and persists the `spec@1`/`plan@1` artifacts the plugins hand off, and compiles the briefings `smith`, `sentinel`, and `scribe` will read. Two different things carried one name across two repositories, and every cross-reference between them had to disambiguate by hand.

## Decision

- The library keeps **Wisp**.
- The plugin ecosystem is **Wisp Plugins**. This is a brand change only: no `plugin.json` `id`, `name`, or version changes; no skill renames; no schema changes.
- In this repository, "Wisp" alone refers to the library. The ecosystem is written "Wisp Plugins" in prose and headings.
- The repository directory and remote name (`agent-plugins`) are unchanged by this ADR.

## Consequences

- `README.md` and any current-facing doc that says "together they're Wisp" says "Wisp Plugins".
- Historical changelog entries and ADR-007's own text stay as written; they record what the brand was when the rename shipped.
- The Wisp library's docs refer to this ecosystem as "Wisp Plugins (`agent-plugins`)". The artifact schemas stay authored here in `shared/schemas/`; Wisp vendors them at a pinned revision with checksums (Wisp D-010).

# Contributing to Wisp

Contributions are welcome. This guide covers the development environment, the invariants every change must keep, and the pull request workflow. By participating you agree to the [Code of Conduct](./CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md). Found a security issue? See [SECURITY.md](./SECURITY.md) instead of opening a public issue.

---

## 1. Development environment

### Prerequisites

- **Toolchain via proto**: `.prototools` pins Rust, moon, just, and cargo-deny. Run `proto use` once.
- **Rust**: 1.96, edition 2024, pinned in `rust-toolchain.toml`.
- **Preferred CLI tools**: `rg`, `fd`, `eza`, `bat`.

### Build and test

```bash
just            # fmt-check + lint + test + audit + doc-check + docs-lint — run before every commit
just test       # workspace tests
just lint       # clippy, -D warnings
just docs-lint  # markdown house style: filler words, fences, D-/Q- references, stale names
```

For one crate use `cargo test -p <crate>` or `cargo clippy -p <crate>` directly, not `moon run <project>:test` — moon's per-project fan-out serializes on the shared `target/` build lock.

### Before opening a PR

CI runs `just ci`. Run it locally first; it is the same pipeline.

---

## 2. Engineering invariants

1. **Safe Rust only.** `unsafe_code = "forbid"`, `unwrap_used`/`expect_used` deny — workspace lints, every crate, no exceptions in library code.
2. **Atomic writes only.** Every canonical artifact write is a same-directory tempfile plus rename. Never write a canonical target in place.
3. **The cache is never the authority.** Nothing under `.wisp/` may be the only copy of a fact. See [`PRINCIPLES.md`](./PRINCIPLES.md).
4. **Implement only what the current gated plan's `covers_criteria` requires.** A spec's `non_goals` are binding. If a task needs scope the spec excludes, stop and raise it.
5. **Spec and plan both gate before implementation.** `scribe:exit-gate` on the spec, `navigator:challenger` on the plan. No `verdict@1` on file means the plan is provisional.
6. **Permissive core stays permissive.** `wisp-contracts` and `wisp-model` are `MIT` and must not depend on any `FSL-1.1-MIT` crate, Tokio, MCP types, Monokl types, SQLite, or CLI formatting.
7. **Docs are unwrapped and unpadded.** One paragraph per line, no emoji, no filler. `just docs-lint` enforces the mechanical part.

The full list, with the reasons, is in [`AGENTS.md`](./AGENTS.md).

---

## 3. Pull request workflow

1. **Branch** with a descriptive name: `feat/…`, `fix/…`, `docs/…`, `chore/…`.
2. **Tests prove criteria.** Every task's tests name the acceptance criteria they cover; mutation testing (`cargo-mutants`) checks the tests would catch real faults.
3. **Verify locally** with `just ci`.
4. **Conventional commits**: `feat:`, `fix:`, `docs:`, `refactor:`, `test:`, `chore:`. The message explains why; the diff already shows what.
5. **Cross-repo dependencies** on Monokl and Michi are `git` + `rev` in committed manifests. A local `[patch]` for path development lives in gitignored `.cargo/config.toml` and never in a commit — see [`docs/07-build-and-release.md`](./docs/07-build-and-release.md).

# Security Policy

## Reporting a vulnerability

Email **security@orin-dx.com** — do not open a public issue for anything exploitable before a fix ships.

Include:

- Which crate is affected (`wisp-contracts`, `wisp-model`, `wisp-schema`, `wisp-artifacts`, `wisp-git`, `wisp-monokl`, `wisp-store`, `wisp-context`, `wisp-output`, `wisp-service`, `wisp-cli`, `wisp-mcp`)
- The concrete failure scenario — what an attacker could do, and how
- A sample artifact, workspace layout, or repro steps if you have them (redact anything sensitive first)

Expect an acknowledgment within 5 business days. We will keep you posted as a fix moves through triage and credit you in the release notes unless you would rather stay anonymous.

## Scope

Wisp reads Git-tracked JSON artifacts, inspects Git state, embeds Monokl to analyze source code, and writes canonical artifacts and a local cache. The relevant threat model:

- **Untrusted artifact JSON** — `wisp-schema` and `wisp-artifacts` parse `spec@1`/`plan@1`/… documents that may come from an untrusted branch or a malicious agent run. A crafted document that escapes the canonical path (`ArtifactId` rejects `/`, `\`, `.`, `..`), bypasses schema validation, or triggers unbounded resource use is a real finding.
- **Repository contents as instructions** — README text, comments, string literals, and copied issue text must never alter Wisp's own validation or persistence policy. Any path by which repository content changes Wisp's behavior beyond being reported as evidence is in scope.
- **Persistence and cache integrity** — canonical writes are atomic (tempfile + rename) and hashed after write; `.wisp/` is derived state. A way to make a receipt report `persisted` for bytes that were not written, or to make a stale cache entry validate as current, is in scope.
- **Git subprocess and `gix` argument handling** — `wisp-git` shells out to `git status` and walks history with `gix`. Path or ref arguments that reach the subprocess unescaped are in scope.
- **Embedded Monokl** — `wisp-monokl` runs Monokl's parsers over workspace source. Parser crashes belong to Monokl's policy; Wisp's handling of Monokl errors and partial results belongs here.
- **MCP surface** — `wisp-mcp`'s tool inputs, especially anything that names a path or an artifact id.
- **Supply chain** — the dependency tree, especially `gix`, `rusqlite` if enabled, and anything `unsafe`-adjacent.

The workspace enforces `unsafe_code = "forbid"`. A report showing that lint bypassed, or a memory-safety bug despite it, is a high-priority finding.

Out of scope: issues in Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, or other harnesses themselves — report those to the platform.

## Supported versions

Wisp is pre-1.0 and unpublished. Security fixes land on `main` only.

      - name: Run CI pipeline

# callisto configuration — see https://github.com/orin-dx/callisto
#
# Release order across the orin-axi repositories is human-tracked (Wisp D-024):
# michi → wisp-contracts → monokl → wisp. Within this repository Callisto orders
# the crates by their dependency graph.

[changesets]
dir = ".changeset"

[cascade]
mode = "out-of-range"
bump-severity = "patch"
peer-escalation = true

# [[package-set]] globs match by package NAME, not directory path, so explicit
# per-crate [[package]] blocks match by path. The workspace still carries
# `publish = false`; these entries describe the intended publication surface and
# take effect when that flag is lifted.

# Permissive interchange layer (MIT). Published first; everything else depends on it.
[[package]]
match = "crates/wisp-contracts"
publish-to = ["crates-io"]
release-trigger = "changeset"

[[package]]
match = "crates/wisp-model"
publish-to = ["crates-io"]
release-trigger = "changeset"

# FSL-1.1-MIT layer.
[[package]]
match = "crates/wisp-schema"
publish-to = ["crates-io"]
release-trigger = "changeset"

[[package]]
match = "crates/wisp-artifacts"
publish-to = ["crates-io"]
release-trigger = "changeset"

[[package]]
match = "crates/wisp-cli"
publish-to = ["crates-io"]
release-trigger = "changeset"

# wisp-fixtures is test-only and never published.
